prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol or other centrally acting D2-blocking antiemetics or antipsychotics; if an antipsychotic is needed, use quetiapine or clozapine
Do not stop lithium abruptly or without psychiatric input to test for a drug cause: abrupt withdrawal raises the risk of manic relapse
Do not prescribe centrally acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) in older adults or in any patient with cognitive impairment
required_recommendations: Diagnose clinically probable PD (MDS 2015): bradykinesia with right-hand rest tremor and rigidity, no absolute exclusion, no red flag; the response to levodopa may add a supportive criterion [Postuma_2015]

Do not attribute the asymmetric rest tremor and parkinsonism to lithium at a therapeutic level (0.72 mEq/L) with normal thyroid function: keep lithium under psychiatric care and monitor the level and renal function, since lisinopril raises lithium levels

Start carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg, half a tablet three times daily with food, increasing over 2 to 4 weeks to one tablet three times daily (300 mg/day levodopa), and review the response after 2 to 3 months, measuring lying and standing blood pressure at each step because tamsulosin adds to orthostatic falls [NICE_NG71]

Prefer levodopa to a dopamine agonist in this man with bipolar disorder; if an agonist is used, warn about impulse control disorders and excessive daytime sleepiness, ask about them and about mood elevation at every visit, and plan it with psychiatry [NICE_NG71]
Advise bedroom safety for the dream enactment (protect his wife, remove sharp objects, pad the bedside); if treatment is needed prefer melatonin, since clonazepam adds sedation and fall risk
Refer for physiotherapy for gait and turning, and for speech and language therapy for the hypophonia

differential.key_features: Lithium for bipolar disorder, but at a therapeutic level (0.72 mEq/L) with normal thyroid function; lithium causes a bilateral postural tremor and only occasionally symmetric parkinsonism, not an asymmetric pill-rolling rest tremor with dream enactment and decrement
Brother with ET and a mild postural tremor component, but the dominant tremor is a 4-5 Hz rest tremor with bradykinesia, decrement, rigidity and micrographia, which ET does not cause
No exposure to antipsychotics or dopamine-blocking antiemetics by history or on the medication list
Asymmetric upper-limb onset with rest tremor; only a few punctate white matter foci (Fazekas 1) on MRI
Dream enactment occurs in MSA, but there is no orthostatic fall, urinary incontinence or cerebellar sign, there is a rest tremor, and the putamina and pons are normal on MRI
Full eye movements, no falls, appendicular rather than axial rigidity, normal midbrain on MRI

key_clinical_evidence: Right-predominant bradykinesia with decrement, cogwheel rigidity and a 4-5 Hz pill-rolling rest tremor of the right hand, with micrographia and hypophonia: parkinsonism with one supportive criterion (rest tremor) and no red flag [Postuma_2015]
No levodopa trial yet and the smell loss is self-reported, so the supportive criteria are not two: clinically probable PD [Postuma_2015]
Wife-witnessed punching and kicking in sleep for 2 years, constipation and reported smell loss: prodromal synucleinopathy markers that lithium does not cause [Berg_2015]
Lithium 0.72 mEq/L with normal TSH and free T4: no supratherapeutic level or hypothyroidism to explain the tremor and slowness
MRI with age-appropriate volume loss and Fazekas 1 foci only: no vascular, NPH, mass or atypical-parkinsonism signature
No orthostatic fall (138/82 supine, 134/80 at 3 minutes) and no urinary incontinence or cerebellar sign

sequence_constraints.reason: Exclude structural and vascular causes on MRI before interpreting a DaTscan [Postuma_2015]

interactions: Lithium causes postural tremor and, less often, parkinsonism. Lisinopril raises lithium levels: keep the level monitored. Levodopa has no pharmacokinetic interaction with lithium.

Tamsulosin (alpha-1 blocker) lowers standing blood pressure and adds to the orthostatic fall; levodopa can lower it further. Review the need for each and measure lying and standing blood pressure at each levodopa dose step.
Lisinopril lowers blood pressure and can add to the orthostatic effect of levodopa.
warnings: Dopaminergic drugs, dopamine agonists in particular, can precipitate hypomania, impulse control disorders or psychosis in bipolar disorder: plan and monitor with psychiatry.
NSAIDs and thiazide diuretics also raise lithium levels; dehydration and intercurrent illness raise the risk of lithium toxicity.
Metformin and atorvastatin: no clinically relevant interaction with levodopa.
High-protein meals can reduce levodopa absorption; distribute protein evenly through the day.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. H is a 69-year-old right-handed Caucasian man who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic for evaluation of a progressive right hand tremor and gait unsteadiness that began approximately 18 months ago. He first noticed an intermittent resting tremor in his right hand while watching television, which initially occurred only during periods of relaxation or stress. Over the following months, the tremor became more persistent and prominent, present both at rest and to a lesser degree with posture. His wife reports that she first noticed the tremor approximately two years ago, before he was aware of it himself. The tremor has progressively worsened and now impairs his ability to eat soup and drink from a cup without spilling. He has also noticed that his handwriting has become smaller and more cramped over the past year, requiring him to print rather than write in cursive. Approximately 10 months ago, he began to notice stiffness in his right arm, particularly in the morning, which improves somewhat with activity but never fully resolves. Six months ago, he developed a shuffling gait with a tendency to stumble, particularly when turning or navigating doorways. His wife reports that he has become slower in his movements overall, taking longer to dress, button his shirt, and get out of a chair. She has also noticed that his facial expression has become less animated and his voice quieter over the past year. He reports occasional constipation that has worsened over the past year and notes a diminished sense of smell that he attributes to aging. He sleeps restlessly, and his wife describes episodes of him acting out dreams, including punching and kicking during sleep, which began approximately two years ago. He denies any cognitive difficulties, hallucinations, changes in mood, urinary incontinence, or significant balance-related falls. He remains independent in all activities of daily living, though tasks take longer than they used to.

neurological_exam.additional: Hoehn and Yahr stage 2.5. Glabellar tap positive (Myerson sign). Seborrhea noted on the forehead. No orthostatic vital sign changes (supine 138/82, standing 134/80 at 3 minutes).
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose accurate bilaterally; the right-hand tremor persists mildly during the movement, without terminal dysmetria or intention tremor. Heel-to-shin testing normal bilaterally.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, reactive to light. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Mild hypomimia with reduced facial expressiveness and decreased blink rate. Facial strength symmetric. Tongue midline without fasciculations. Palate elevates symmetrically.
neurological_exam.gait: Gait is narrow-based with reduced stride length and mildly shuffling quality. Reduced right arm swing, with left arm swing preserved. Mild difficulty initiating gait from standing position. Turns require 4-5 steps (increased from normal 2-3). Pull test shows 2 steps retropulsion but recovers independently. No festination. Tandem gait is difficult but performed with effort.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. MMSE 29/30 (lost 1 point on delayed recall). Mild bradyphrenia noted with delayed responses to open-ended questions. Speech is hypophonic but fluent with intact comprehension and repetition. No evidence of hallucinations or delusions.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone: moderate cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist and mild rigidity at the left wrist. Mild rigidity at the right elbow. No rigidity at ankles. Strength 5/5 in all extremities bilaterally. Prominent resting tremor of the right hand at 4-5 Hz, pill-rolling quality, which dampens with voluntary movement. Mild postural tremor of the right hand when arms are outstretched. No tremor of the left hand at rest; very subtle intermittent postural tremor of the left hand. Rapid alternating movements are slow and decremental on the right, mildly slow on the left. Finger tapping shows progressive decrement in amplitude and speed on the right.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign. No jaw jerk.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact throughout. Vibration sense mildly reduced at the bilateral great toes, consistent with age. Joint position sense intact at the great toes bilaterally.
